metadata.title: Product Streams
metadata.description: Outcome-based product streams for the Instant Photo Book Platform domain, modeled on PastBook: the creation journey from discovering the app or pastbook.com, importing photos from the phone, a computer, Dropbox, Google Drive or Facebook, AI curation and automatic design in under 60 seconds, optional editing and checkout in seven currencies; the production journey from print-ready files routed to partner facilities on four continents to shipped, tracked parcels within the published delivery windows and 24/7 support with reprints; and the growth and operations journeys (seasonal campaigns, yearbook reminders and reorders, the global print partner network, photo privacy and platform compliance) that keep a 1-click photo book business with 10M+ books created running.
metadata.flowModelNote: Each stream carries only stream-specific flows, names the supporting bricks used in each step and the persona acting in it (or the platform when a step is automated), and lists the external systems (Meta Graph API and Facebook Login, Apple App Store and Google Play, Dropbox and Google Drive, payment providers, partner printing facilities, carriers, messaging gateways, review platforms, advertising and attribution partners) the flow depends on. Prices, delivery windows, review figures and company facts are the sourced PastBook figures from September 2026; mechanics of curation, routing and compliance are modeled.

rootGroups.name: Create a Book
rootGroups.description: From the first ad or App Store feature to a paid order: install the app or open pastbook.com, import photos from the phone, a computer, Dropbox, Google Drive or Facebook, let the AI curate and design the book in under 60 seconds, preview for free, optionally edit and personalise, and check out in one of seven currencies. These journeys decide preview-to-order conversion, the minutes from opening the app to ordering and the acceptance of the automatic selection.

streams.name: Discover and Install the App
streams.description: Take a consumer from the first encounter with PastBook - a paid social ad, an App Store feature (PastBook was featured in several countries in September 2022), the GQ gift guide, a Trustpilot review or a friend's book on the coffee table - to an installed PastBook 1-Click Photo Book app (1M+ downloads on iOS and Android) or a first visit to pastbook.com, with the photo-library permission granted and a first book started. The app store listing, the ten-language website and the in-app onboarding all repeat one promise: a book in under 60 seconds without designing. Attribution ties the install and the first order back to the campaign so the Growth Marketer can steer CAC and ROAS across countries, with about 80% of customers in the United States.
outcomes: An interested consumer reaches an installed app or an open web creator in one session, with photo permission granted and the first import started
Every install and first order is attributed to a campaign, store placement or referral so acquisition spend is judged on orders, not clicks
Onboarding explains the 60-second promise, the free preview and the pay-per-book model so nobody expects a subscription or a design tool

streams.name: Import Photos from Phone and Cloud
streams.description: Turn the customer's photo sources into an indexed photo set the curation engine can work on: the phone camera roll selected by date, location, album or Yearbook mode in the iOS and Android app, and folders uploaded from a computer, Dropbox or Google Drive in the web creator. Only the selected photos are uploaded, over encrypted connections, with timestamps, locations and EXIF metadata preserved so moments can be grouped later; originals are stored in the media store behind a CDN and deleted according to the privacy policy. Since Instagram discontinued third-party access for personal accounts, the phone and cloud drives have become the primary sources next to Facebook, so import reliability across tens of thousands of photos and slow mobile networks decides whether the 60-second promise holds.
outcomes: A parent with 30,000 photos can select a year, a school year or a holiday in seconds and see the upload finish while the AI is already working
Every uploaded photo keeps the timestamp, location and orientation the curation and layout engines need, and nothing is uploaded that the customer did not select
Uploads survive app switches, lost connections and large folders from Dropbox or Google Drive without duplicating or losing photos

flows.title: From Camera Roll to an Indexed Photo Set
flows.description: A parent picks a school year or holiday in the app; the app scans the camera roll, uploads the selected photos over an encrypted connection and hands an indexed set to curation.
flows.trigger: The customer taps 'Create a book' and chooses a date range, location, album or Yearbook mode.
flows.successSignal: All selected photos are uploaded, indexed with time, place and orientation, and curation has started.

steps.title: Choose date range, location, album or Yearbook mode
keyFacts: Yearbook mode proposes one book per calendar year; date, location and album modes let the customer narrow to a holiday, a city or an existing album.
The app shows the photo count per selection so the customer knows whether 400 or 4,000 photos go into the book.
painPoints: Camera rolls mixed with screenshots, WhatsApp images and receipts inflate the count and the upload time.
Albums synced from iCloud shared libraries sometimes appear empty in limited-access mode.

dependencies.how: Scans the camera roll index and offers date, location, album and Yearbook selections with counts.

dependencies.name: Mobile App Shell (iOS and Android)
dependencies.how: Renders the selection screens and counts.

steps.title: Scan the camera roll on device and pre-filter
keyFacts: The app reads the local photo index (timestamps, locations, media type) on device and excludes videos, screenshots and images below a minimum resolution before anything leaves the phone.
On-device pre-filtering reduces the upload volume and keeps clearly unusable images out of the book.
painPoints: iCloud-optimised libraries keep only thumbnails on the phone, so full-resolution downloads slow the scan on poor networks.
Live Photos and HEIC formats must be converted without losing colour or orientation.

dependencies.name: Photo Library Access and Import

steps.title: Upload the selected photos over encrypted connections
keyFacts: Selected photos are uploaded in parallel over TLS with resumable chunks; the upload continues in the background and resumes after a lost connection or an app switch.
Each upload carries the original EXIF metadata (time, GPS, orientation, camera) that curation and layout need.
painPoints: Thousands of full-resolution photos on a mobile network can take longer than the 60-second curation itself.
iOS background limits kill long uploads when the customer leaves the app.

dependencies.name: Photo Library Access and Import

steps.title: Index time, place and orientation for every photo
keyFacts: The indexer normalises timestamps to the customer's time zone, reverse-geocodes GPS to place names and fixes orientation from EXIF so the book reads in chronological order.
Photos without timestamps (forwarded WhatsApp images) are placed by file date and flagged for the curation engine.
painPoints: Time zone shifts on a trip put evening photos on the next day's page.
Reverse-geocoding is unavailable for photos without GPS, so trip books lose place captions.

steps.title: Confirm the photo set and start curation
keyFacts: The app shows the final count, the date span and a few thumbnails; confirming hands the set to the curation engine while remaining uploads finish.
Curation starts on the photos already uploaded so the 60-second clock is not waiting for the last file.
painPoints: Customers who add photos after confirming expect them to appear in the already designed book.
Partial uploads that fail silently lead to books missing a whole day of a holiday.

flows.description: A traveller with a folder of trip photos on a laptop or in Dropbox uploads it to the web creator; the platform de-duplicates against earlier uploads and indexes the set.

steps.title: Connect Dropbox or Google Drive or pick local files
keyFacts: Dropbox and Google Drive are connected through OAuth file pickers scoped to the chosen folders; local files are selected with a drag-and-drop area that accepts JPEG, PNG and HEIC.
Only the selected folders are read; the OAuth token is stored as a source connection and revoked on request.
painPoints: Google Drive folders shared by a partner sometimes contain low-resolution thumbnails instead of originals.
Browser uploads of 2,000 files from a laptop stall when the tab is put in the background.

steps.title: Upload the files and de-duplicate against earlier uploads
keyFacts: Files are hashed in the browser before upload so exact duplicates already in the customer's media store are skipped; the rest is uploaded in parallel over TLS.
Large folders are uploaded in the background while the customer can already see the first thumbnails.
painPoints: Edited exports of the same photo have different hashes and are only caught later by near-duplicate detection.
Corporate laptops with strict proxies block the parallel upload endpoints.

steps.title: Index the set and fix metadata gaps
keyFacts: Folder names and file dates are used when EXIF is missing, which is common for photos exported from messaging apps or older cameras.
The customer can set a date span or a place for the whole set so the book still reads chronologically.
painPoints: Scanned prints and photos from a friend's camera with a wrong clock end up out of order.
Without location data, trip books lose the place-based moment grouping that makes them feel curated.

keyFacts: A grid shows the imported photos with the count and date span; the customer can remove screenshots or someone else's photos before curation runs.

Source connections remain linked to the project so a later re-import of a Dropbox folder is a one-click action.

streams.name: Connect Facebook and Pick a Year
streams.description: Take a Facebook user from Facebook Login to a book of one year of their timeline: albums, timeline pictures, cover and profile photos and mobile uploads with their captions and dates, grouped per year from 2009 to 2025, imported within the permission scope Meta allows. The flow runs on pastbook.com as Facebook Photo Books and is the main channel for the Facebook Timeline Archivist, an older and price-sensitive customer who wants 'my 2016' in one click. Since Instagram discontinued third-party tools for personal accounts, Facebook is the only social source left, so every Meta app review, permission change and token expiry directly affects a product line. Facebook data is used only for the book and deleted on request under Meta Platform Terms.
outcomes: A connected Facebook account shows a year picker with photo counts per year within seconds, and a chosen year becomes a book with captions and dates
Facebook import completion rate stays high despite rate limits, expired tokens and permission changes, and every failure explains what to do
PastBook stays compliant with Meta Platform Terms: minimal permissions, data used only for the order, deletion on request and a passed app review at every change

flows.title: From Facebook Login to a Year of Photos
flows.description: A Facebook user logs in, grants photo permission, sees photo counts per year 2009-2025, picks a year and watches albums, timeline, cover and profile photos with captions being imported.

steps.title: Log in with Facebook and grant the photo permission
keyFacts: Facebook Login requests the user_photos permission (and the public profile) that Meta grants to reviewed apps; the customer sees exactly which data PastBook will read.
The token is stored as a source connection with its expiry and scope; nothing else on the profile is read.
painPoints: Customers who decline the photo permission but complete the login land in an empty creator.
Meta's permission dialogs change with app review cycles and break screenshots in the help center.

steps.title: Count photos per year from 2009 to 2025
keyFacts: The importer reads album, timeline, cover and profile photo and mobile-upload metadata and shows the number of photos per year so the customer picks a year with enough material.
Counting reads metadata only, not the image files, to stay within Graph API rate limits.
painPoints: Accounts with 15 years of photos need many paginated Graph API calls and hit rate limits during Q4 peaks.
Photos the customer is tagged in but did not upload are not available and customers expect them.

Years with few photos are flagged as likely to yield a softcover of up to 16 pages.
painPoints: Customers pick a year with 40 photos and are disappointed by a thin book.
Profile and cover photos repeat across years and inflate the count.

steps.title: Import the year's photos with captions and dates
keyFacts: Images are downloaded server-side from the Graph API at the largest available size, with caption text, post date and album name attached to each photo.
Import runs in the background with progress shown; the customer can start previewing when the first albums are in.
painPoints: Facebook serves compressed images, so print quality depends on the largest available rendition.
Tokens expiring mid-import leave a half-imported year without a clear recovery path.

streams.name: Curate the Best Photos with AI
streams.description: Turn thousands of photos into the best moments in under 60 seconds with the patent-pending curation engine launched in the AI app in July 2021: score every image for blur, exposure and resolution, detect duplicates and near-duplicates from burst shots and edited exports, group photos into moments by time, place and people, and rank the best photo per moment so the book tells the year without the customer reviewing 5,000 images. Curation is PastBook's differentiator against on-device memories from Apple and Google and against AI tools at Mixbook and Popsa; its quality decides the photo selection acceptance rate, the share of customers who edit, the reprint rate and the gross margin. Analysis runs on uploaded photos in the region of the customer and never on data the customer did not select.
outcomes: A book from 3,000 photos is curated in under 60 seconds with blurry, dark and duplicate shots removed and every important moment represented
Photo selection acceptance rate rises so most customers order without editing, and the curation learns from every swap and removal
Curation quality is measurable per source and country and can be improved with experiments without changing the app

flows.title: From Thousands of Photos to the Best Moments in 60 Seconds

steps.title: Score every photo for blur, exposure, resolution and faces
keyFacts: Each photo gets a quality score from blur, exposure, noise, resolution and face detection (open eyes, faces cut off); the score is stored with the photo asset for reuse.
Scoring runs in parallel on the uploaded derivatives in the customer's region so a 3,000-photo set finishes in seconds.
painPoints: Artistic low-light or motion photos from a concert are scored as bad and dropped.
Face detection on children's photos requires strict handling: scores only, no identity, no retention beyond the project.

steps.title: Detect duplicates, bursts and near-duplicates
keyFacts: Exact duplicates are found by hash; near-duplicates (bursts, edited exports, the same scene ten times) are found by perceptual similarity within a time window and clustered.
From each cluster only the best-scored photo is kept as a candidate; the rest are marked as alternatives for the editor.
painPoints: Near-duplicate thresholds that are too strict merge different group photos of the same wall.
Panoramas and collages confuse similarity models.

keyFacts: Photos are grouped into moments from time gaps, location changes and recurring faces: a birthday afternoon, a weekend in Lisbon, the first day of school.
Moments are labelled with the date and place used for chapter pages and captions.
painPoints: A 16-hour flight day and a short beach trip produce moments of very different sizes.
Photos without location or with a wrong camera clock land in the wrong moment.

keyFacts: Selection balances quality score, moment coverage, people variety and orientation mix to fill the target book (24 pages by default, more when the year is rich) so every moment is represented.
The target count respects the cover rules: books above 300 pages fall back to softcover, so the selection caps pages unless the customer asks for more.
painPoints: Filling 24 pages from a 40-photo year produces one photo per page and looks empty.
Over-representing one child in a two-child family is the most common complaint about automatic selection.

Pipeline failures must fall back to a simpler chronological selection rather than an error.

painPoints: Small segments (Brazil, New Zealand) have too few orders per week for stable rates.
Seasonal Year in Review books behave differently from trip books and skew the average.

Experiments are stratified by source and country and run until acceptance and conversion are significant.
painPoints: Experiments in Q4 risk the peak; most run in quieter months on smaller volume.

streams.name: Auto-design the Book and Preview
streams.description: Turn the curated moments into a finished book without the customer designing anything: the smart layout generator places photos on page designs that fit orientation and importance, adds dates, places and captions, the theme engine picks cover and colour palette from the photos, and the customer sees a free preview of the whole book within the same 60 seconds. streams.name: Edit and Personalise the Book

rootGroups.name: Produce and Deliver
rootGroups.description: From a paid order to a book in the customer's hands and a resolved problem when something goes wrong: render and preflight print-ready files, route to the nearest partner facility with capacity on four continents, produce on FSC-certified paper, ship and track within the published windows per country, and run 24/7 support with reprints, refunds and a reply to every negative review within 48 hours.

streams.name: Render Print-ready Files and Route to a Printer
streams.description: Turn a paid order into files a partner can print without questions: render the frozen design version into print-ready PDFs with bleed, spine width by page count and colour profiles, impose pages for the partner's press, preflight for resolution, fonts, overflow and colour, and route the job to the partner facility nearest the customer that has capacity and the right product, on one of four continents. Production starts on payment, so rendering and routing run within minutes, and the routing rules balance delivery window, unit cost, quality history and peak capacity. The job goes out with order data, a packing slip and the shipping method, and print file rejection rate at partners is the measure of how well this stream works.
outcomes: Every paid order becomes imposed, preflighted files at the right partner within minutes, without manual work in the control tower
Print file rejection rate at partners stays near zero because preflight catches resolution, font, bleed and spine issues first
Routing keeps most orders produced in the customer's country, balances peak capacity and picks the lowest cost partner that meets the delivery window

streams.name: Produce, Ship and Track the Order
streams.description: From a routed job to a parcel in the customer's hands within the published windows after production: United States 4-8 business days, United Kingdom 4-5, France, Netherlands, Italy and Germany 3-5, rest of EU 5-7, Canada and Australia 5-10, New Zealand, India and Brazil 7-10. The partner prints on FSC-certified paper, binds hardcover or softcover, produces calendars and posters, checks quality, packs with the packing slip and hands the parcel to the carrier with a label PastBook created; tracking events flow back to the order page, the app and the shipping e-mails, and the SLA monitor compares every step with the promise. Multi-product orders ship on the longest production time, and in Q4 the stream carries the gift givers whose north star is gifts delivered before the occasion.
outcomes: Orders are produced, shipped and delivered within the published windows and the customer can see where the parcel is at any moment
On-time production and shipping rate and print defect rate are visible per partner and per country and trigger action before customers complain
Delivery exceptions (lost, damaged, returned) are detected from carrier events and resolved proactively, especially before holiday deadlines

painPoints: Paper stock changes at the partner alter spine width and colour without notice.
Peak volumes in December stretch press time and eat into the delivery window.

streams.name: Resolve Support Requests and Reprints
streams.description: Give every customer one contact that solves the problem: 24/7 support agents in the Netherlands, United States, Sri Lanka and India answer on WhatsApp, e-mail and chat, with the help center for self-service in ten languages. Agents change addresses, answer tracking questions, fix Facebook and upload problems, judge print-quality complaints from photos and preflight reports, and decide on reprint, refund or a goodwill discount; reprints go back through rendering and routing with priority. Every negative Trustpilot review (2% one-star of 35,837 reviews) gets a public reply typically within 48 hours, and complaint causes are fed back to the curation, preflight and partner teams. First-contact resolution rate is the north star, with median first response time and reprint rate as supporting KPIs.
outcomes: Most contacts are resolved in one conversation because the agent sees the order, design, preflight report, partner status and tracking in one place
Reprints and refunds are decided within clear rules, produced with priority and traced to a root cause (curation, preflight, partner, carrier, customer)
Every negative public review gets a reply within 48 hours and complaints turn into fixes for product, partners and the help center

rootGroups.name: Grow and Run the Network
rootGroups.description: The operator journeys that keep the business growing and compliant: seasonal campaigns and promotions in ten languages with a Q4 peak, yearbook reminders and reorders that build an annual memory habit, the global print partner network with SLAs, capacity and quality, and the privacy and platform compliance that protects personal photos and the Meta, app store and payment relationships the product depends on.

streams.name: Run Seasonal Campaigns and Promotions
streams.description: Run the acquisition and promotion engine that made PastBook grow 10x year-on-year for three years and win the Deloitte Fast50 2019: paid social and search, App Store optimisation and featuring, e-mail and push campaigns in ten languages and seven currencies, with promo codes and free-shipping upgrades that run continuously and peak steeply in Q4 around Black Friday, Christmas and the Year in Review campaign. About 80% of customers are in the United States while costs are in euros, so campaign budgets, prices and creative are managed per country and attributed to installs and orders through the measurement partner. The Growth Marketer's north star is blended customer acquisition cost, with return on ad spend and install-to-order conversion as supporting KPIs; campaigns must also respect app-store rules, Meta advertising policies and consent.
outcomes: Campaigns launch in ten languages and seven currencies from one calendar, with codes, prices and creative consistent from ad to checkout
Blended CAC and ROAS are known per country and channel within days, and budget moves to the campaigns that produce orders, not installs
The Q4 peak is planned with production capacity and support staffing so a successful campaign does not break delivery promises

steps.title: Plan the campaign, budget and targets per country
keyFacts: The plan sets dates, countries, channels, budget and CAC and ROAS targets per country; the US takes most of the budget, followed by Australia, Europe and the UK.
Q4 plans are aligned with production capacity per region and support staffing, because a campaign that sells more than partners can print creates late gifts.
painPoints: Euro-based costs against USD revenue expose the plan to exchange rates.

flows.title: From a Platform Policy Change to a Compliant Release
flows.description: Policy changes from Meta, Apple, Google and payment providers are monitored, assessed for product impact, implemented and taken through app review and data-use checks.
flows.trigger: Meta, Apple, Google or a payment provider announces a policy, API or review change, or an app release is planned.
flows.successSignal: The change is implemented, the release passes review, privacy labels and data-use checks are current and no policy incident occurs.

steps.title: Monitor Meta, app store and payment policy and API changes
keyFacts: Developer announcements, Graph API version deprecations, App Store and Google Play policy updates and payment provider rule changes are tracked with dates and impact.
Instagram's discontinuation of third-party access for personal accounts is the reference case for why monitoring matters.
painPoints: Announcements come through many channels and are easy to miss.
Deprecation timelines are sometimes shorter than a release cycle.

dependencies.name: Integration Gateway
dependencies.how: Tracks API versions and deprecations per platform.

dependencies.name: Privacy, Consent and Data Deletion (GDPR, CCPA)
dependencies.how: Records policy changes and compliance obligations.

dependencies.name: Analytics and Experimentation
dependencies.how: Sizes the share of orders affected by a channel.

steps.title: Assess impact on products, data use and permissions
keyFacts: Each change is assessed for affected products (Facebook Photo Books, app, payments), data use, permissions and customer communication; Facebook Photo Books depends on the user_photos permission remaining available.
Keep the app and integrations compliant with platform policies is the platform partner's first job.
painPoints: A permission loss can end a product line, as Instagram showed.
Assessments need product, legal and engineering in one room quickly.

dependencies.name: Privacy, Consent and Data Deletion (GDPR, CCPA)
dependencies.how: Records the assessment and required actions.

dependencies.name: Facebook Connect and Year Selector
dependencies.how: Identifies affected Facebook flows and scopes.

dependencies.how: Identifies affected payment flows.

steps.title: Implement changes and update privacy labels and data-use forms
keyFacts: The app and integrations are updated; App Store privacy labels, Google Play data safety forms and Meta's data-use checkup are refreshed to match actual data flows.
Changes to consent texts follow the same release.
painPoints: Privacy labels that do not match SDK behaviour cause review rejections.
Meta's annual data-use checkup can suspend the app if missed.

dependencies.how: Implements app-side changes for the release.

dependencies.name: Privacy, Consent and Data Deletion (GDPR, CCPA)

steps.title: Submit for app review and platform approval
keyFacts: The release is submitted to App Store and Google Play review; Meta app review is requested for permission or scope changes; test accounts and screencasts are prepared.
Review timing is planned around campaign launches and store featuring.
painPoints: Rejections a week before Black Friday delay the campaign.
Meta review requires a working demo with real Facebook data.

dependencies.name: Mobile App Shell (iOS and Android)

dependencies.how: Manages the Meta review submission.

steps.title: Keep payments compliant with provider rules and PCI DSS scope
keyFacts: Card data never touches PastBook systems; tokenisation and 3-D Secure are handled by providers, and the yearly PCI self-assessment reflects that scope; dispute and refund rules follow provider terms.
Provider rule changes (strong customer authentication, currency support) are implemented in checkout.
painPoints: Chargeback ratios above provider thresholds threaten the account.
Seven currencies mean seven sets of local payment rules.

steps.title: Communicate changes to customers and support
keyFacts: When a change affects customers (a source lost, a permission re-consent), the help center and in-app messages explain what changed and what to do, as the Instagram page did.
Support agents receive the explanation before the release.
painPoints: Customers blame PastBook for platform decisions.
Silent changes create support spikes.
